title: The routine of a Gursikh
hookLine: Guru Ram Das's salok on the Guru's Sikh: up early, bathed, remembering the Name (Gauri Var M4, ang 305)

cards: Whoever calls himself a Sikh of the Guru. That's how a short salok begins, in Guru Ram Das's ballad in Raga Gauri. Notice the opening.
Not whoever was born into a Sikh family. Not whoever knows the hymns by heart. Whoever claims the name.
And instead of a definition, the salok hands you a clock: what that claim looks like before the sun is up. A new voice on the path, Guru Ram Das, whose hymns carry the heading Mahala four.
The first thing we hear from him is a morning.

teach.h: A NAME TURNS INTO A HABIT.
teach.b: The first half of the salok, paraphrased: the one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru rises in the early hours and dwells on the Lord's Name.
He makes the effort, early in the morning, bathes, and dips in the pool of nectar. Following the Guru's teaching, he repeats the Name, and his faults and wrongs fall away. Three things stand out.
First, a name turns into a habit. The salok doesn't argue about who counts as a Sikh. It describes a morning and lets the morning answer.
Second, the word for effort, udam. Rising early isn't a personality type for the lucky few who wake up cheerful. It's something you make the effort to do, the way a farmer gets up to water a field.

teach.h: THE POOL OF NECTAR, BODY AND MIND.
BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE GETS A VOTE.
teach.b: Some readers hear a real bath, the body washed before the day. Others hear the pool as the Name itself, where the mind gets washed. Some teachers hold both together.
Sikhs call those early hours amrit vela, the ambrosial time, a phrase from Guru Nanak's Japji.
The salok itself doesn't name the sangat, but for Sikhs near a gurdwara, the morning can mean walking in to hear the prayers with others.
So the routine of a Gursikh isn't a rulebook. It's a person whose day starts with remembering, on purpose, before anything else gets a vote.

how: Sikhs who keep the daily discipline rise in the early hours, bathe, and recite the morning prayers, beginning with the Japji; this salok of Guru Ram Das is one of the passages Sikh teachers turn to when they describe the Sikh day.

games.q: what does “the routine of a gursikh” mean?
o: rising early to bathe and remember the Name
the order of hymns sung at a gurdwara each day
a strict list of rules for joining the Khalsa

games.q: the salok's morning: tap the pairs.
p: a bath, and the Name that washes

s: the salok defines a Sikh by birth into a Sikh family
it begins with whoever calls himself a Sikh of the Guru, then describes a morning.
the salok names effort as part of rising early
he makes the effort, early in the morning: udam.
every reader takes the pool of nectar only as a literal bath
some hear a real bath, others the Name itself; some teachers hold both.

games.q: someone says they're a Sikh of the Guru. the salok wants to know what that looks like. what does it describe?
o: a list of beliefs to sign.
a morning: rise, bathe, remember the Name.
games.why: it hands you a clock, not a definition: the early hours, the effort, the bath and the Name.

practice: Imagine tomorrow's first minutes at a time a little earlier than usual, not heroic, just a little.

Choose what the first thing will be, washing your face slowly, a line of Gurbani, a few quiet breaths before the phone, and hold that picture until it feels doable. If you pray, let Waheguru be the first word in it.

wordCard.voice: The routine of a Gursikh. Guru Ram Das's salok: rise early, make the effort, bathe, and dwell on the Name before the day begins. Today's word.

orig.note: a Sikh of the Guru: the person the salok describes, from the moment they rise.

carryVoice: Your line: the gursikh's morning. The day can start with remembering, before anything else gets a vote. See you tomorrow.
